stimulus.text:
“This Constitution, and the Laws of the United States which shall be made in Pursuance thereof; and all Treaties made, or which shall be made, under the Authority of the United States, shall be the supreme Law of the Land; and the Judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any Thing in the Constitution or Laws of any State to the Contrary notwithstanding. . . . no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.”

—Constitution of the United States, Article VI, September 17, 1787
stimulus.source_note: Constitution of the United States, Article VI, September 17, 1787. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Constitution of the United States, Article VI, September 17, 1787, public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.9 The Constitution, Federalism—the National Government and the States

primary_sources: Constitution of the United States, Article VI (September 17, 1787)

stem: The passage says “no religious Test shall ever be required as a Qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.” What does that rule most directly mean?

options.text: Only members of one church may hold federal office.
options.misconception: A religious test would pick one faith; the passage forbids any such test.

options.text: Federal officeholders must swear an oath on a Bible.
options.misconception: The passage forbids a religious test, so it cannot require a Bible oath.

options.text: A person’s religion cannot bar them from federal office.
Churches may not own property in the United States.
options.misconception: The passage is about holding office, not about churches owning property.

rationales.C: If no religious test may be required, then religion cannot be used to keep a person out of office.
rationales.A: One church only would itself be a religious test, which the passage forbids.
rationales.B: Requiring a Bible oath would be a religious test, which the passage forbids.
rationales.D: The passage covers qualifications for office, not church property.
rationales.general:
1. A religious test is a rule that a person must hold a certain faith to take office.
2. The passage says no such test “shall ever be required” for any federal office.
3. So a person’s religion cannot be used to bar them from serving.
4. The rule says nothing about church property, which is a different matter.
Remember: “no religious test” means faith is not a qualification for office.
